subject: ela
skillName: Develop and strengthen writing through planning, revising, editing
intro: Each item gives you a short paragraph or a brief draft to work with. Read it closely, then decide how to revise or edit it so the writing gets stronger. Some questions ask you to choose the best change, some ask which sentence to cut or add, and some ask you to fix a convention error in context. Always keep the writer's meaning.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Our school garden is a great place to learn. Students grow tomatoes, beans, and herbs there. The garden teaches kids where food comes from. My cousin plays the trumpet in band.' Which sentence should the writer cut during revision, and why?
items.answer: The writer should cut 'My cousin plays the trumpet in band,' because it is about band, not about the school garden, so it does not support the paragraph's topic.

steps: Find the paragraph's main idea: the school garden is a good place to learn.
Check each sentence against that topic. The first three are all about the garden and what it teaches.
The sentence 'My cousin plays the trumpet in band' is about a cousin and music, not the garden.
Cutting the off-topic sentence keeps the paragraph focused, so it is the one to remove.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from a draft: 'The storm was bad and the storm was loud and the storm scared the little kids.' Which revision is the strongest improvement?
A) The storm was bad, and it was loud, and it scared the little kids.
B) The loud storm frightened the little kids.
C) The storm, which was bad, was loud and scared the kids.
D) The storm was very bad and very loud and scary.
items.answer: B) The loud storm frightened the little kids.

steps: The original repeats 'the storm' three times and uses the vague word 'bad.'
Option B combines the ideas into one clear sentence and replaces 'bad' and 'scared' with the precise word 'frightened.'
Options A, C, and D keep the repetition or stay wordy and vague, so they do not improve clarity as much.
The concise, precise version in B is the best revision.

items.prompt:
Read this short draft: 'Reading every day helps you in school. It builds your vocabulary so you understand harder texts.' The writer wants to add one sentence that develops the paragraph. Which sentence best develops it?
A) Some people like to read at night before bed.
B) Reading also improves your writing because you see how good authors put words together.
C) Reading every day is something that helps you in school a lot.
D) My favorite book is about a dragon and a knight.
items.answer: B) Reading also improves your writing because you see how good authors put words together.

steps: The paragraph's topic is how reading every day helps you in school.
Option B adds a new, relevant benefit (better writing) and explains why, which develops the idea.
Option A and D are off topic, and option C just repeats the main idea without adding support.
B is the only choice that adds real, on-topic support.

items.prompt: A writer revises a paragraph by moving the topic sentence from the end to the beginning so readers see the main idea first. Is this change revising or editing, and why?
items.answer: It is revising, because moving a sentence to improve the order and organization changes the structure of the writing, not just a surface convention.

steps: Editing fixes surface conventions like spelling, capitalization, and punctuation.
Revising changes ideas, content, or organization.
Reordering sentences so the main idea comes first changes how the paragraph is organized.
Because it affects organization, this is revising, not editing.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from a student draft: 'we visited the museum on friday and saw the dinosaur bones.' Which edited version corrects the convention errors without changing the meaning?
A) We visited the museum on Friday and saw the dinosaur bones.
B) We visited the Museum on friday and saw the dinosaur bones.
C) we visited the museum on Friday, and saw the Dinosaur bones.
D) We visited the museum on friday and seen the dinosaur bones.
items.answer: A) We visited the museum on Friday and saw the dinosaur bones.

steps: The original needs a capital 'We' to start the sentence and a capital 'Friday' for the day of the week.
Option A capitalizes both and keeps the meaning exactly the same.
Option B leaves 'friday' lowercase and wrongly capitalizes 'Museum.' Option C leaves 'we' lowercase and wrongly capitalizes 'Dinosaur.'
Option D adds a grammar error ('seen' instead of 'saw'), so A is the only correct edit.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Honeybees are important to farmers. They move pollen from flower to flower, which helps fruits and vegetables grow. Without bees, many crops would produce far less food.' Where should the writer add the transition word 'For example' to improve the flow?
items.answer: The writer should add 'For example' to the start of the second sentence: 'For example, they move pollen from flower to flower, which helps fruits and vegetables grow.' This signals that the sentence gives a specific way bees are important to farmers.

steps: The first sentence states the main idea: honeybees are important to farmers.
The second sentence gives a specific example of how they are important.
Adding 'For example' at the start of that second sentence shows the reader it is illustrating the main idea.
This transition makes the connection between the general claim and the example flow more clearly.

items.prompt:
Read this draft: 'The hiking trail was nice. The trees were nice and the view at the top was nice.' Which revision best improves the word choice?
A) The hiking trail was nice, and the trees and the view were nice too.
B) The hiking trail was peaceful, with tall pine trees and a sweeping view at the top.
C) The hiking trail was really very nice in every single way.
D) The trail was nice because the trees were nice and so was the view.
items.answer: B) The hiking trail was peaceful, with tall pine trees and a sweeping view at the top.

steps: The original repeats the weak word 'nice' three times.
Option B replaces 'nice' with precise, vivid words like 'peaceful,' 'tall pine,' and 'sweeping,' and combines the details smoothly.
Options A, C, and D keep the vague word 'nice' or just add more words without making it clearer.
B is the strongest improvement for word choice.

items.prompt: Read this paragraph: 'Skateboarding is good exercise. It builds balance and leg strength. Riders also learn to focus and keep trying after they fall. A helmet protects your head.' Which sentence is least connected to the paragraph's main idea that skateboarding is good exercise, and should be cut or moved?
items.answer: The sentence 'A helmet protects your head' is least connected, because it is about safety gear, not about how skateboarding is good exercise, so the writer should cut it or move it to a paragraph about safety.

steps: The main idea is that skateboarding is good exercise.
The first three sentences describe physical and mental benefits of skateboarding.
The sentence about a helmet is about safety equipment, which is a different topic.
Because it does not support the exercise idea, it should be cut or moved to a safety paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read this two-sentence draft: 'My little brother is annoying. He sings the same song over and over until everyone in the house has it stuck in their head.' A reader says the first sentence is vague. Which revision best sharpens the main idea?
A) My little brother is so annoying that it is unbelievable.
B) My little brother has an annoying habit that drives the whole family crazy.
C) My little brother is kind of annoying sometimes, I think.
D) My little brother is annoying and he is also loud.
items.answer: B) My little brother has an annoying habit that drives the whole family crazy.

steps: The original 'My little brother is annoying' is vague because it does not say how.
The second sentence shows the annoying habit is repeating a song, so the topic sentence should point to a habit.
Option B names 'an annoying habit' that affects 'the whole family,' which matches the detail and sharpens the idea.
Options A, C, and D stay vague or add an unrelated point, so B is best.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from a draft: 'After the long game the players was tired and they goes home.' Which edited version fixes the grammar errors without changing the meaning?
A) After the long game, the players were tired and they went home.
B) After the long game the players was tired and they went home.
C) After the long game, the players were tired and they goes home.
D) After the long game the players are tired and they go home.
items.answer: A) After the long game, the players were tired and they went home.

steps: The subject 'players' is plural, so the verb should be 'were,' not 'was.'
The action already happened, so 'goes' should be the past tense 'went.'
Option A fixes both verbs and adds a comma after the opening phrase, keeping the meaning the same.
Options B, C, and D each leave at least one verb error or change the time, so A is correct.

items.prompt:
Read this draft: 'There are many reasons to recycle. It saves energy. It keeps trash out of landfills.' During revising, the writer wants to combine the two short sentences into one smoother sentence. Which revision is best?
A) It saves energy, it keeps trash out of landfills.
B) Recycling saves energy and keeps trash out of landfills.
C) It saves energy and also it keeps the trash out of the landfills too.
D) There are many reasons to recycle, and it saves energy and trash.
items.answer: B) Recycling saves energy and keeps trash out of landfills.

steps: The two short sentences each give one reason to recycle.
Option B joins them with 'and' into one clear sentence and names 'Recycling' as the subject.
Option A uses a comma splice, option C is wordy and repetitive, and option D blurs the meaning by saying 'energy and trash.'
B combines the ideas smoothly without adding errors, so it is the best revision.

items.prompt: A writer is planning a report about volcanoes. They list every fact they can think of, then group the facts into 'how volcanoes form,' 'famous eruptions,' and 'staying safe.' Which stage of the writing process is the writer in, and how do you know?
items.answer: The writer is in the planning (prewriting) stage, because gathering ideas and grouping them into categories happens before drafting, to organize what will be written.

steps: Planning, or prewriting, is when a writer gathers and organizes ideas before drafting.
Here the writer lists facts and sorts them into groups.
No draft has been written yet, and no conventions are being corrected.
Because the writer is organizing ideas before drafting, this is the planning stage.

items.prompt:
Read this paragraph: 'The new park has a lot to offer. The basketball court is always busy. Families picnic on the grass. There are shady benches for reading.' The writer wants to add a strong closing sentence. Which sentence best fits and develops the paragraph?
A) Parks are found in many cities across the country.
B) With so many activities, the new park has something for everyone.
C) The basketball court is always busy, as I said before.
D) I have never actually been to the new park myself.
items.answer: B) With so many activities, the new park has something for everyone.

steps: The paragraph lists several activities the new park offers.
Option B sums up those activities and ties back to the main idea that the park has a lot to offer.
Option A is a general fact about parks everywhere, option C just repeats a detail, and option D contradicts the confident tone.
B is the on-topic closing sentence that develops the paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from a draft: 'Me and Jordan studyed for the test all weekend.' Which edited version corrects the errors without changing the meaning?
A) Jordan and I studied for the test all weekend.
B) Me and Jordan studied for the test all weekend.
C) Jordan and me studyed for the test all weekend.
D) Jordan and I study for the test all weekend.
items.answer: A) Jordan and I studied for the test all weekend.

steps: The subject of the sentence needs 'I,' not 'Me,' and the polite order puts Jordan first: 'Jordan and I.'
'studyed' is misspelled and should be 'studied.'
Option A fixes the pronoun, the order, and the spelling while keeping the meaning.
Options B and C keep a pronoun or spelling error, and option D changes the time to present tense, so A is correct.

items.prompt: Read these scrambled sentences from a draft about making a sandwich: (1) 'Finally, put the top slice of bread on and cut it in half.' (2) 'First, lay two slices of bread on a plate.' (3) 'Next, spread peanut butter on one slice and jelly on the other.' To revise for organization, what order should the sentences be in, and why?
items.answer: The correct order is 2, 3, 1, because the steps must follow the real sequence: first lay out the bread, next spread the fillings, and finally put the top slice on and cut it. The transition words 'First,' 'Next,' and 'Finally' signal that order.

steps: The paragraph explains steps for making a sandwich, so the sentences should follow the order of the steps.
Sentence (2) begins with 'First' and lays out the bread, so it goes first.
Sentence (3) begins with 'Next' and adds the fillings, so it goes second.
Sentence (1) begins with 'Finally' and finishes the sandwich, so it goes last, giving the order 2, 3, 1.
